title: LoadBalancer – Cloud‑Ready Exposure ☁️
description: Get a public IP for your Service using a cloud provider’s load balancer.

slides.title: What is LoadBalancer? ☁️
slides.content:
# The production standard for external access

A LoadBalancer Service type provisions an **external load balancer** from your cloud provider (AWS ELB, GCP Cloud LB, Azure LB) and assigns a public IP. It also creates a ClusterIP and NodePort internally.

Ideal for:
- Public‑facing web applications
- APIs consumed by external clients
- Any service that needs a stable, public endpoint

slides.title: LoadBalancer YAML 📝
slides.content:
## Almost identical to NodePort

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: web-lb
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer
  selector:
    app: web
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 8080
```

No `nodePort` needed – the cloud provider allocates one automatically and sets up the load balancer to forward to it.

slides.title: Create and Wait for External IP
slides.content: In a cloud cluster (or with a local LB solution like MetalLB):
slides.codeSnippet:
kubectl apply -f web-lb.yaml
kubectl get services web-lb --watch
# Wait until EXTERNAL-IP is no longer <pending>

quizData.question: What happens if you create a LoadBalancer Service on a local cluster without a cloud provider?

options.text: It uses a default public IP

quizData.explanation: Without a cloud controller or MetalLB, the LoadBalancer external IP will never be assigned.

slides.title: Internal Load Balancers 🏢
slides.content:
## Not always public

Cloud providers also support **internal** load balancers (private IPs within your VPC). You annotate the Service:

```yaml
metadata:
  annotations:
    service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-internal: "true"
```

This creates a load balancer reachable only inside your VPC – great for internal APIs.

slides.title: Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content:
## Use an Ingress for HTTP(S) traffic

Instead of creating a LoadBalancer per Service (expensive), use an **Ingress** (Chapter 8) that routes by hostname/path to multiple ClusterIP Services through a single load balancer.

quizData.question: Why use an Ingress instead of many LoadBalancer Services?

options.text: Ingress reduces cost by sharing one load balancer across multiple Services

quizData.explanation: Ingress consolidates routing, saving cloud LB costs and simplifying management.

slides.title: MetalLB for Bare‑Metal ⚙️
slides.content:
## Get LoadBalancer on‑premise

If you run Kubernetes on bare‑metal or VMs, you can install **MetalLB** – a software load balancer that assigns IPs to Services of type LoadBalancer. It works by announcing IPs via ARP/NDP or BGP.

This gives you LoadBalancer functionality without a cloud provider.

quizData.question: True or False: MetalLB can provide LoadBalancer Services on a bare‑metal cluster.
quizData.explanation: MetalLB implements the LoadBalancer interface for on‑premise clusters.
